section_summaries.epidemiology: Leishmaniasis is a complex of sandfly bite-transmitted protozoan parasitic disease, endemic to nearly 100 countries across five continents, and is considered a neglected tropical disease. Visceral leishmaniasis (VL) is often associated with poverty, while cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) tracks with conflict and population movement. The disease is transmitted by female sandflies of the genera Phlebotomus (Old World) and Lutzomyia (New World). Sandflies are weak fliers, inactive in daylight, and breed in damp, organic matter-rich places. They feed on various warm- and cold-blooded hosts, including humans, and can transmit Leishmania after 7-10 days, remaining infective for weeks. Leishmania-infected sandflies exhibit abnormal feeding behavior, potentially facilitating transmission. Transmission can be zoonotic (mammalian reservoirs like dogs, rodents) or anthroponotic (human reservoirs). Globally, in 2015/2016, there were an estimated 4 million new CL cases, 61,000 new VL cases, and 13,700 deaths, with about a billion people at risk. CL is endemic in over 70 tropical and neo-tropical countries, with most cases reported from Afghanistan, Algeria, Brazil, Colombia, Iran, Pakistan, Peru, Sudan, Syrian Arab Republic, Tunisia, and Yemen. VL cases are predominantly from Brazil, Ethiopia, India, Kenya, Somalia, South Sudan, and Sudan. Other transmission routes include blood transfusion, needle sharing among drug users, congenital transmission, and laboratory accidents. In Old World CL, infections are common in semi-arid or desert ecologic zones, often a childhood disease. L. major is a zoonotic infection of desert rodents, while L. tropica can be zoonotic or anthroponotic. L. aethiopica is a zoonotic parasite with rock and tree hyraxes as reservoirs. New World CL involves adaptation to peri-domestic environments, with increasing urbanization and human movement into endemic areas leading to new infections. L. mexicana is transmitted by Lutzomyia olmeca; L. amazonensis is primarily a disease of forest rodents; L.(V.) braziliensis, L.(V.) guyanensis, and L.(V.) panamensis are associated with humans in farming communities, with sloths as reservoirs for some species; L.(V.) peruviana in high Andean valleys has dogs as principal reservoirs.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: Promastigotes are introduced into the skin by infected female sandflies during a blood meal. They invade reticulo-endothelial cells and transform into amastigotes, which multiply within phagolysosomes. Infected cells rupture, and amastigotes invade other reticuloendothelial cells. Ingested by sandflies, amastigotes transform into promastigotes in the gut and migrate to the proboscis. The protective immune response is primarily cell-mediated, with antibodies having little role in host defense for VL. A positive leishmanin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay correlates with resistance. Cell-mediated immunity can also cause tissue destruction. A protective immune response involves IL-12, interferon-gamma, and TNF-alpha in VL, and IL-2, IL-12, and interferon-gamma in CL. Macrophages kill amastigotes via reactive oxygen species and nitric oxide. Memory T cells and CD8 T cells are important for durable immune responses in CL, while IL-10 and TGF-beta are associated with active VL or persistent CL. Poor nutrition and immunocompromised states are major risk factors. Leishmania RNA viruses, particularly in South America, have been associated with ML and antimony-unresponsive CL/ML. After sandfly inoculation, promastigotes enter and multiply in reticuloendothelial cells, spreading to local lymph nodes and then hematogenously to liver, spleen, and bone marrow. This results in outcomes from asymptomatic infection to disseminated VL. Sub-clinical cases or lymphatic leishmaniasis show non-caseating granulomas and giant cell reaction. Bone marrow often contains parasite-laden macrophages. In fatal cases, skin is heavily infiltrated with parasitized cells around sweat glands and arterioles. Disease development depends on parasite strain, inoculum, host immune responses, and sandfly factors. Host inflammatory responses mediate disease expression, leading to self-healing ulcerative CL or chronic, non-healing diffuse CL, ML, or leishmaniasis recidivans. CMI generally mediates resolution. Leishmaniasis recidivans shows a granulomatous reaction with scanty parasites, while diffuse CL involves a CMI defect with numerous parasite-filled macrophages. In immunocompromised hosts, especially with AIDS or solid organ transplant, diffuse CL involves abundant parasites, but its pathogenesis differs.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: Leishmaniasis presents in three general syndromes: visceral leishmaniasis (VL), cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL), and mucosal leishmaniasis (ML). VL (Kala-azar) is characterized by irregular fever, wasting, pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, and hypergammaglobulinemia, with some patients showing hyperpigmentation. Atypical or sub-clinical VL is common, with missing clinical features. VL is caused by L. donovani complex parasites. CL presents as localized, non-healing, often ulcerative skin lesions, with less common nodular, psoriasiform, or verrucous forms. Other cutaneous syndromes include diffuse CL, disseminated CL, post-Kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL), and leishmaniasis recidivans. ML, common in New World CL from L. (Viannia) braziliensis, L.(V.) guyanensis, and L.(V.) panamensis, involves destructive nasopharyngeal lesions. Old World ML-like syndromes are associated with L. major, L. infantum, and L. aethiopica. Clinical syndromes can also be classified by parasite burden: polyparasitic (VL, diffuse CL) with many parasites, and oligoparasitic (ML, leishmaniasis recidivans) with fewer. VL incubation is typically 2-6 months; onset can be acute (high fever, chills, malaise) in immunologically naïve adults or gradual (chronic intermittent fever, progressive hepatosplenomegaly, weight loss, epistaxis, diarrhea, cough) in endemic areas. Patients are often weak and emaciated, with distended abdomen from splenomegaly/hepatomegaly. Lymphadenopathy, edema, jaundice, petechiae, and purpura may occur. Immunocompromised hosts may have gastrointestinal involvement, mucosal lesions, or disseminated skin lesions. Uncommon systemic manifestations include retinal hemorrhages, hepatic necrosis, pancytopenia without splenomegaly, cholecystitis, and paresthesias. Laboratory abnormalities include anemia (5-9 g/dL), leukopenia (2000-4000/mm³), thrombocytopenia (50,000-200,000/mm³), eosinophil absence, elevated ESR, mildly elevated liver transaminases, prolonged prothrombin time, low serum albumin (<3 g/dL), and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (5-10 g/dL, mostly IgG). Renal defects can occur. Complications include bacterial pneumonia, pulmonary tuberculosis, HIV co-infection, cancrum oris, and ocular complications (retinal hemorrhages, keratitis, uveitis). VL in HIV-infected patients is an opportunistic infection, usually with CD4 <100/mm³, presenting similarly to non-HIV hosts but with more fever, less organomegaly, leukopenia, and more GI involvement. PKDL presents after VL treatment as macules and papules around the mouth, spreading to the face and extensor surfaces, appearing as hypopigmented patches or nodules resembling leprosy. CL incubation is 2-8 weeks (up to 3 years), starting as an inflammatory papule that may become a plaque or nodule, then an ulcer with serous fluid and crust, surrounded by an indurated, discolored area. Lesions are typically on exposed body parts. L. major lesions are larger, multiple, inflamed, crusting, and heal in months. L. tropica lesions are smaller, fewer, develop slowly, and persist for a year or more. L. infantum lesions are small and nodular. L. aethiopica lesions are chronic, least inflamed, self-healing in 2-5 years, often localized nodular, but can cause oronasal leishmaniasis or diffuse CL. Leishmaniasis recidivans is a rare, chronic form of CL, typically on the face, with progressing lupoid papules/nodules around healed scars, persisting for 20-40 years, causing destructive disfigurement. Diffuse CL (L. aethiopica, L. mexicana, L. amazonensis) begins as a single non-ulcerating nodular lesion, followed by disseminated cutaneous macules, papules, nodules, plaques, or diffuse infiltration, resembling lepromatous leprosy. These lesions do not ulcerate and are chronic and relapsing. New World CL progresses similarly to Old World, with initial papules becoming scaly or ulcerated. L. mexicana infections are often few, self-healing in 6 months, but chronic on the ear. L.(V.) braziliensis complex lesions heal in 6-18 months but can persist longer, with lymphadenopathy. L. guyanensis infections involve multiple skin lesions, and L.(V.) panamensis infections show sporotrichoid subcutaneous nodules. DL (L.(V.) braziliensis or L. amazonensis) in immunocompetent persons involves hundreds of pleomorphic skin lesions and up to 44% mucosal involvement. ML (espundia) is a metastatic complication of New World CL, primarily L.(V.) braziliensis, affecting 5-10% of infected persons, months to years after skin lesions heal. It starts with nasal stuffiness/breathing difficulty/epistaxis, progressing to septum ulceration and mutilating destruction of the nasal septum, palate, lips, pharynx, and larynx. ML is chronic, progressive, and can be fatal.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Definitive diagnosis requires demonstrating amastigotes by histopathology, special culturing, or molecular methods. There is no single optimal diagnostic test, so multiple parasitologic assays (smear, culture, PCR) are preferred. Promastigotes can be grown in various media at 22-25°C, usually within 2-7 days in Schneider's medium or 7-21 days in NNN medium. Molecular-based assays are the most sensitive approach, with whole-blood PCR having 93% sensitivity and 95.6% specificity, and are also used for species identification and MALDI mass spectrometry. Clinical diagnosis of VL can be made presumptively in endemic areas using serologic tests (e.g., rK39 immunochromatographic test) if invasive procedures are difficult, but confirmatory parasitologic diagnosis is preferable. For parasite demonstration, specimens are obtained from bone marrow, liver, spleen, or lymph nodes. Splenic aspiration has the highest sensitivity, with smears stained with Giemsa's or Leishman's demonstrating amastigotes in >95% of cases. Bone marrow aspiration is preferred due to safety concerns with splenic aspiration, but smears show fewer amastigotes (50-85% positive). Culture and PCR are needed for light parasite burdens. Serologic tests for VL include ELISA, immunofluorescence (IFA), and direct agglutination test (DAT) using whole promastigotes, crude lysates, or recombinant antigens. These tests have >90% sensitivity but lower specificity, with false positives possible (malaria, trypanosomiasis, tuberculosis). IFA is positive in >95% of VL patients. DAT sensitivity/specificity estimates are 94.8%/85.9%. Recombinant protein rK39 is used in rapid diagnostic tests (93.9% sensitivity, 90.6% specificity). rK39 is not for asymptomatic screening. Differential diagnosis of late-stage VL includes hematologic/lymphatic malignancies, disseminated histoplasmosis, hepatosplenic schistosomiasis. Early VL differential includes malaria, African trypanosomiasis, brucellosis, enteric fevers, bacterial endocarditis, chronic myelocytic leukemia, Hodgkin's disease, lymphomas, sarcoidosis, hepatic cirrhosis, tuberculosis, and hyper-reactive malaria splenomegaly. For CL, typical ulcerative lesions are cleaned, anesthetized (lidocaine-epinephrine), and crust debrided. Samples are obtained by scraping for smears, culturing, or PCR testing (95% ethanol). Tissue fluid aspirates or biopsies (with impression smears) can also be used. Low titers of anti-leishmanial antibodies are detected in many CL patients, but standard serologic tests are generally not diagnostically helpful. Differential diagnosis of CL includes pyoderma, cutaneous myiasis, rickettsial eschar, tropical ulcer, tertiary syphilis, yaws, lupus vulgaris, blastomycosis, sporotrichosis, chromomycosis, cutaneous actinomycosis, pyoderma gangrenosum, spider bites, fixed drug eruptions, lichen simplex chronicus, basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma. For ML (espundia), differential diagnoses include paracoccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis, tuberculosis, syphilis, malignant tumors, lethal midline granuloma. Nodular diffuse CL must be differentiated from lepromatous leprosy. PCR is an essential tool for pauciparasitic ML diagnosis.
section_summaries.treatment: Treatment varies by Leishmania species, geography, host factors, and syndrome. Miltefosine and liposomal amphotericin B have largely replaced traditional pentavalent antimony therapy. Cure is defined clinically (resolution of signs/symptoms) or parasitologically (parasite eradication, less common). VL clinical cure is resolution of fever, improved well-being, anemia, splenomegaly, and weight gain over months, with no relapse at 6 months. CL clinical cure is complete epithelialization of an ulcer at 3 months, without recurrence up to 6 months. Viable parasites may persist after clinical cure. Non-specific supportive care for VL includes a nutritious diet, antimicrobials for co-infections (pneumonia, TB), blood transfusions for severe anemia (hemoglobin <6 g/dL), vitamin supplements, and assessment for HIV co-infection or other immunosuppression. Specific anti-leishmanial therapies include Pentavalent Antimonials (SbV), Amphotericin B, Paromomycin, and Miltefosine. SbV (sodium stibogluconate, meglumine antimoniate) is given intravenously (20 mg/kg/day for 28 days) or intramuscularly. It can cause nausea, anorexia, abdominal pain, malaise, headache, rash, arthralgias, myalgias, lethargy, pancreatic enzyme elevations, renal tubular acidosis, acute renal failure, and lymphopenia. ECG abnormalities are common, and SbV is contraindicated in pregnancy. Amphotericin B deoxycholate (1 mg/kg every 1-2 days for total ~20 mg/kg) is used for SbV failures, but has infusion-related side effects and long-term renal/hematologic issues. Liposomal amphotericin B (L-amB) (3 mg/kg daily for 5 doses, then days 14, 21 for total 21 mg/kg in immunocompetent, or 4 mg/kg daily for 5 doses then days 10, 17, 24, 31, 38 for total 40 mg/kg in immunosuppressed) is the drug of choice for VL, with >90% success rate (higher doses in East Africa). Single 10 mg/kg L-amB dose is >95% efficacious for L. donovani in India. Paromomycin (15 mg/kg intramuscularly for 21 days) has 93-95% cure rates in Indian VL, and 85% in East Africa (20 mg/kg). Miltefosine (oral, 2.5 mg/kg/day for 28 days; adult dosing based on weight for 28 days) is FDA approved for L. donovani VL, with 95% cure in India and ~90% in Ethiopia. It causes GI side effects and is teratogenic. Drug resistance is a growing concern. Combination treatments (e.g., SbV + paromomycin; L-amB + miltefosine; L-amB + paromomycin; miltefosine + paromomycin) are used to shorten duration, reduce dose, mitigate toxicity, and reduce resistance, achieving 98-99% cure rates in India. Relapses, common 2-6 months post-treatment, require different drug regimens or higher/additional doses. PKDL treatment (depending on severity) includes extended amphotericin B deoxycholate (1 mg/kg/day for 60-80 doses over 4 months) or miltefosine (50 mg TID for 60 days, or 100 mg/day for 90 days/12 weeks). In East Africa, most PKDL self-heals, but severe/disfiguring cases are treated with SSG + paromomycin or L-amB. For HIV-associated VL, L-amB is preferred, followed by HAART for immune reconstitution and secondary prophylaxis. SbV and miltefosine are contraindicated in pregnancy; L-amB is the best option. Old World CL lesions often self-heal. Local therapies include thermotherapy, cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen), photodynamic therapy, topical paromomycin, intralesional SbV, and combinations. Systemic treatment is indicated for large/multiple lesions or those in cosmetically/functionally important areas. SbV (20 mg/kg/day IM/IV for 10-20 days) is used; fluconazole (200-400 mg daily for 6 weeks) has modest efficacy for L. major. Leishmaniasis recidivans treatment involves SbV (15-20 mg/kg/day IM/IV for 15 days) plus oral allopurinol (20 mg/kg for 30 days), or other therapies like miltefosine or L-amB. New World CL generally requires systemic chemotherapy due to severity and mucosal disease risk. SSG (20 mg/kg/day for 20 days) is recommended. Amphotericin B deoxycholate (1 mg/kg on alternate days for 2-3g total) is effective for SbV-unresponsive cases. L-amB is increasingly used. Pentamidine (2-3 mg/kg every other day for 4-7 doses) is effective for L.(V.) panamensis or L.(V.) guyanensis. Ketoconazole (70% cure for L.(V.) panamensis) and fluconazole have variable efficacy for New World CL. Oral miltefosine (2.5 mg/kg/day for 28 days) is approved for New World CL from L.(V.) braziliensis, L.(V.) guyanensis, and L.(V.) panamensis, and ML from L.(V.) braziliensis, with variable cure rates. Local agents like thermotherapy and topical paromomycin formulations are also used. ML treatment recommendations include SbV (20 mg/kg/day IM/IV for 30 days), SbV + oral pentoxifylline, amphotericin B deoxycholate (0.7-1 mg/kg on alternate days for 25-45 doses), L-amB (2-3 mg/kg/day for total 40-60 mg/kg), or miltefosine (2.5-3.3 mg/kg/day for 28 days). Advanced ML requires nutritional support and sometimes plastic surgery.
section_summaries.prevention: There is no vaccine or chemoprophylaxis. Personal protective measures include protective clothing, DEET-based insect repellents, and permethrin-treated clothing/bed nets. Aggressive case management helps interrupt anthroponotic transmission. Needle exchange programs reduce transmission among injecting drug users. Leukodepletion reduces transfusion-associated risk. PKDL patients can act as chronic human reservoirs. Reservoir control for zoonotic VL (L. infantum) in dogs is challenging; studies on dog culling and residual insecticide spraying lack randomized controlled trials, but topical insecticides (deltamethrin-impregnated collars) show individual protection. Vector control reduces incidence by improved sanitation, refuse removal, and residual insecticide spraying (e.g., DDT), though efficacy for CL in all settings is not fully evidenced. Immunization (leishmanization with live L. major promastigotes) was historically used in Russia, Israel, and Iran to induce a single scar and immunity, but carries risks of CL lesions requiring treatment or leishmaniasis recidivans, and theoretical risk for immunocompromised individuals. For New World CL/ML, vaccines and chemoprophylaxis are unavailable. Control is difficult due to forest vectors/reservoirs, except for uta (L.(V.) peruviana) which can be minimized by house spraying and personal protection.
